extracted.intended_audience: voters and citizens of New York (and the general public) evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition assessing the particular structure and distribution of powers in the proposed federal Constitution, focusing on separation of legislative, executive, and judicial functions and the practical checks needed to prevent usurpation. It contrasts theory (Montesquieu) with practice (State constitutions, risks of legislative encroachment, and militia vs standing army arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of representatives to favor local over national interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A great proportion of the errors committed by the State legislatures proceeds from the disposition of the members to sacrifice the comprehensive and permanent interest of the State, to the particular and separate views of the counties or districts in which they reside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that both state and federal legislatures are liable to decide measures according to local prejudices, interests, and pursuits rather than national prosperity; cautions that members will often act as partisans of their states/districts rather than impartial guardians of a common interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: State governments and popular sentiment as effective checks on federal encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: If an act of a particular State... be generally popular in that State ... it is executed immediately and, of course, by means on the spot and depending on the State alone. The opposition of the federal government... would but inflame the zeal of all parties on the side of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies concrete modes of resistance available to States and their people: public disquietude, refusal to cooperate with federal officers, executive disfavor, obstructive legislative devices, inter-State correspondence and concerted plans of resistance; argues these offer powerful, readily available checks against federal overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implausibility of federal accumulation of a standing military force as a means of usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: The only refuge left for those who prophesy the downfall of the State governments is the visionary supposition that the federal government may previously accumulate a military force for the projects of ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that forming a regular army sufficient to overpower the States is unlikely and would itself be resisted; supplies rough proportions (highest standing army ≈ 1/100 of souls; militia in U.S. could amount to near half a million) to show militia superiority in numbers and attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia plus local governments chosen by the people form a superior barrier against tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of subordinate governments, to which the people are attached, and by which the militia officers are appointed, forms a barrier against the enterprises of ambition... it may be affirmed with the greatest assurance, that the throne of every tyranny in Europe would be speedily overturned... .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stresses qualitative advantages: militia officered by local choices, fighting for common liberties, united by governments possessing popular confidence; combined with local governments these make successful domestic usurpation unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of the federal government on the people as a safeguard (either/or argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the mode in which the federal government is to be constructed will render it sufficiently dependent on the people, or it will not. On the first supposition, it will be restrained by that dependence... On the other supposition, it will not possess the confidence of the people, and its schemes of usurpation will be easily defeated by the State governments...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents a dichotomy: dependence secures restraint because of accountability; independence deprives the federal government of public support, making resistance by States and people effective. Used as a concise conclusive form of the anti-usurpation argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct interpretation of Montesquieu's maxim on separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's meaning ... can amount to no more than this, that where the WHOLE power of one department is exercised by the same hands which possess the WHOLE power of another department, the fundamental principles of a free constitution are subverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects an absolutist reading that requires total independence of departments; uses the British Constitution as Montesquieu's exemplar to show that partial agency and reciprocal controls between departments are consistent with the maxim, so long as the whole powers are not united in the same hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute separation of powers is impracticable; partial mixtures are common and often necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If we look into the constitutions of the several States, we find that ... there is not a single instance in which the several departments of power have been kept absolutely separate and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents many explicit examples from State constitutions (e.g., Senate as tribunal for impeachments, executive presiding in Senate, appointment/removal overlaps) to show that constitutions accept qualified mixtures—separation 'as the nature of a free government will admit'—and that total separation is neither observed nor always desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation of all powers in the same hands is the definition of tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands... may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that tyranny can result whether powers are vested in one, a few, or many; plurality does not prevent oppression (an 'elective despotism'); thus the constitutional design must prevent any single entity from exercising whole powers of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative department is particularly prone to encroachment and requires special precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative department derives a superiority ... Its constitutional powers being at once more extensive, and less susceptible of precise limits, it can, with the greater facility, mask ... the encroachments which it makes on the co-ordinate departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists reasons why legislature is dangerous: broader and less precisely defined powers, access to public coffers (purse strings), influence over appointments and salaries, and facility to hide encroachments within complex measures; supports claim with examples from Virginia (Jefferson) and Pennsylvania (Council of Censors) showing legislative usurpations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parchment barriers are insufficient—departments must have constitutional control over each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless these departments be so far connected and blended as to give to each a constitutional control over the others, the degree of separation which the maxim requires ... can never in practice be duly maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for practical, mutual constitutional checks (appointment, impeachment, removal, vetoes, shared functions) rather than relying solely on precise enumeration of boundaries; supplies historical/state examples where lack of practical checks led to violations of constitutional prescriptions.
